headline: Connecticut leaders oppose proposed Head Start overhaul as comment period closes
dek: Gov. Ned Lamont, Attorney General William Tong and early-childhood commissioner Elena Trueworthy say proposed federal changes could weaken standards serving about 5,600 Connecticut children and families. The public-comment period closed Tuesday.
body: Connecticut’s top early-childhood officials are asking the Trump administration to withdraw a proposed rewrite of the federal Head Start rules, putting the state in direct opposition to a plan whose public-comment period closed Tuesday, Oct. 6. Gov. Ned Lamont, Attorney General William Tong and Office of Early Childhood Commissioner Elena Trueworthy announced their position Tuesday and said Connecticut submitted written comments to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

The [Connecticut governor’s office](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-urges-trump-administration-to-withdraw-proposal-to-overhaul-head-start) described the proposed rule as a broad reduction in federal performance standards. The [Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/07/2026-16134/reducing-federal-burden-for-head-start-programs) says the Administration for Children and Families wants to replace the standards last revised in 2024, reduce federal administrative requirements and defer to state policies where possible. The notice sets Oct. 6 as the deadline for public comments; it does not make the proposal final.

The changes under debate reach into the daily operation of Head Start and Early Head Start. Connecticut officials said the proposal would reduce requirements covering teaching and learning, staffing, group size, coaching and professional development. It would also remove some suspension and expulsion protections and lower the allowable administrative-cost cap from 15% to 5% of a program’s approved costs. The federal notice frames those changes as a way to reduce bureaucracy and move more resources toward direct services, while acknowledging that programs may need to change how they allocate money and staff.

The local stakes are substantial even though the rule would be written in Washington. The governor’s office says Head Start serves about 5,600 Connecticut children from birth through age 5 and their families. The program includes preschool for children ages 3 to 5, Early Head Start for infants and toddlers, services for pregnant women and home-visiting options. A [Connecticut Mirror report](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/02/head-start-1002/) citing the state Office of Early Childhood’s 2024-25 data counted 4,847 children and pregnant women participating in 34 federally funded programs, a measure that uses a different population and reporting period than the governor’s current estimate.

Supporters and opponents describe the tradeoff differently. HHS has said the proposal would expand access, reduce unnecessary federal bureaucracy and give local providers more flexibility, while retaining requirements for health, disability, family and school-readiness services, according to CT Mirror. Connecticut advocates and lawmakers argue that loosening class-size, staffing and disability-service rules could make it harder for programs to provide consistent care, particularly to children with disabilities, children experiencing homelessness or housing instability, children in foster care and families who face language or other access barriers. [WFSB’s report](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/06/state-leaders-push-back-proposed-head-start-changes/) said state leaders were urging residents to weigh in before the deadline.

The timing also intersects with Connecticut’s own expansion of early-childhood programs. Lamont’s office said the state deposited $411.7 million in surplus funds into a new Early Childhood Education Endowment in June, bringing its value above $700 million. The state’s Early Start CT program is scheduled to expand in July 2027, with free care planned for eligible families earning up to $100,000 and a 7% household-income contribution cap for some families above that level. State officials say weaker federal Head Start standards could create gaps in a system Connecticut is trying to build out.

Nothing in Tuesday’s announcement changes Head Start services immediately. The federal agency must first review the public record and decide whether to revise, withdraw or finalize the proposed rule. Connecticut’s letters call for preserving federal standards while pursuing narrower ways to reduce paperwork. Until HHS takes that next step, the practical question for families and providers is not whether the overhaul has taken effect, but how the final rule will treat the staffing, language, disability and family-support requirements that make Head Start more than a preschool program.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Connecticut leaders oppose proposed Head Start overhaul
seoDescription: Connecticut leaders are urging the Trump administration to withdraw proposed Head Start changes after the public-comment period closed.
